body: Feedback can sting, even when it is fair. For about ninety days you will receive one short note a day to help you hear comments without crumbling, and to turn them into something useful.
Today, just notice what happens inside you when someone offers a comment on your work or behaviour. No judging, only noticing.
Think of the last piece of criticism that stayed with you. How long did it echo? Hours, days, longer?
Most people react to feedback in one of a few ways: defending, collapsing, deflecting with a joke, or going cold. Which feels most familiar?
Feedback is information about how something landed for one person. It is not a final verdict on your worth.
Notice where the sting of criticism sits in your body. A hot face, a tight throat, a sinking feeling? Simply name it.
Today, pay attention to praise as well. Do you brush it off quickly? How we take compliments often mirrors how we take criticism.
Ask yourself what you fear a critical comment might reveal. That you are not good enough, not liked, not capable? Write it down honestly.
Remember a piece of feedback that annoyed you at the time but helped later. What changed between hearing it and using it?
The first reaction to criticism is rarely the wisest one. Let today be about noticing that first wave without acting on it.
Notice the difference between feedback on what you did and comments about who you are. The first is usually far easier to work with.
Think of someone whose opinion you trust. How would you feel about hearing a gentle criticism from them compared with from a stranger?
Watch how often you replay a comment in your head. Each replay tends to make it louder than it was.
Notice whether you seek out feedback or avoid it. Avoiding it can feel safer, but it also keeps you guessing.
Two weeks in. What has surprised you most about your reactions to comments and corrections? Note one honest observation.
First small practice: next time you hear a criticism, say only "Thank you, let me think about that." Nothing more is needed in the moment.
Practise the pause. When a comment stings, take one slow breath before you speak. The urge to defend usually softens a little.
Try asking one clarifying question about a piece of feedback today, such as "Could you give me an example?"
Write the feedback down in plain, neutral words. Stripping out the tone often shows you the useful part underneath.
Separate the message from the delivery. Someone can make a fair point badly. You can still take the fair point.
Today, ask for feedback on something small and low-stakes, like a short email or a dish you cooked. Notice how it feels to invite it.
When you feel the urge to explain why you did something, hold it back for a moment. Hear the whole comment first.
Sort a recent piece of criticism into three piles: true, partly true, not true. Most feedback has at least a grain in the first two.
Notice the stories you add to feedback. "They said the report was long" can quickly become "They think I'm useless." Stick to what was said.
Practise saying "That's useful to know" even when you are not yet sure it is. It keeps the conversation open while you think.
Give yourself a set amount of time to feel the sting of a comment, perhaps ten minutes. Then turn your attention to what you can do with it.
Try thanking someone for honest feedback, even if it was hard to hear. It takes courage to give, too.
Notice your self-talk after criticism. Would you speak to a friend that way? If not, try a kinder sentence.
Today, look for one tiny improvement you can make based on recent feedback. Small, quick changes help the comment feel useful rather than heavy.
Remember that you can take time. Very little feedback requires an instant response or an immediate change.
A month in. Think of a recent comment you handled a little better than you would have before. What did you do differently?
Ask someone you trust: "What is one thing I could do better?" Then simply listen and say thank you.
Notice if you dismiss feedback by questioning the person who gave it. Sometimes the source matters, but the point may still be worth checking.
Keep a short note of useful feedback you receive. Over time, patterns appear that no single comment could show you.
Practise hearing feedback without immediately apologising at length. A brief "Thanks, I'll work on that" is often enough.
When you feel defensive, get curious instead. Ask yourself what you might be missing, and what they might be seeing.
Try receiving a compliment today with a simple "Thank you." No deflecting, no downplaying. Notice how that feels.
Remind yourself that being criticised does not mean you are disliked. People who care often say harder things.
If a comment really hurts, it may be touching on something you already worry about. That is worth knowing, gently.
Today, look for the specific behaviour in a piece of feedback. Something you can change is far easier to act on than a vague impression.
Notice how your mood affects how feedback lands. On a tired day, a mild comment can feel enormous. Factor that in.
Practise asking "What would good look like to you?" It turns criticism into a clearer target.
When you disagree with feedback, you are allowed to. Try "I see it a bit differently, here's why" after you have listened properly.
After a hard conversation about your work, do something steadying before you return to it. A short walk, a cup of tea, some fresh air.
Feedback from one person is one data point. If several people say the same thing, it is worth giving it more weight.
Six weeks done. Which practice has helped most so far: pausing, writing it down, asking questions? Lean on it this week.
Now for harder ground. Think of a piece of feedback you have been avoiding acting on. What is one small first step?
Practise asking for feedback on something you care about deeply. Expect it to feel more uncomfortable, and do it anyway.
When feedback comes from someone close to you, notice the extra sting. Remind yourself they are commenting on an action, not on your bond.
Try hearing feedback in a group setting without shrinking or bristling. Sit up, breathe, and take notes if you can.
If you were once criticised harshly in the past, notice when a new comment echoes that old one. The present person may mean something milder.
Today, follow up on a piece of feedback you acted on. Let the person know what you changed. It builds trust both ways.
Practise staying open when feedback is delivered clumsily or sharply. Look past the tone for anything you can use.
Notice whether you over-correct after criticism, changing everything at once. One thoughtful adjustment is usually wiser.
When feedback feels unfair, wait a day before replying. Then decide calmly whether to discuss it, accept part of it, or let it go.
Ask yourself what you would do with this comment if your ego were not involved at all. That answer is often the useful one.
Practise asking for feedback before a piece of work is finished. Early comments are easier to hear and easier to use.
Think about a mistake that was pointed out to you recently. Can you own it plainly, without beating yourself up or making excuses?
Notice whether you treat praise as luck and criticism as truth. Try weighing them both with the same fairness.
Today, give someone else a piece of kind, specific feedback. Seeing it from the other side can soften how you receive it.
Two months in. Which kind of feedback used to floor you that now feels more manageable? Take a moment to notice that change.
Try reading an old piece of criticism again. Does it look different now that some time and distance have passed?
Practise hearing "no" or "not good enough yet" as a stage in the work rather than an ending.
When you feel crushed by a comment, list three things you know you do well. It puts the feedback in proportion.
Notice the difference between a growing pain and a real warning sign. Most feedback is the first kind.
Today, ask a colleague or friend how they handle criticism. You might pick up a useful habit or two.
If a review or appraisal is coming up, prepare by listing what you are proud of and what you want to improve. Go in curious.
Practise saying "You might be right" when you are genuinely unsure. It shows openness without giving up your own judgement.
After receiving feedback, decide on one action and one thing to let go. Not every comment needs a response.
Pay attention to how you speak about feedback afterwards. Telling it fairly to a friend, without spin, helps you hear it fairly too.
Notice how much lighter work feels when you stop dreading every comment. Even a little less dread is real progress.
Think of the people whose growth you admire. Most of them have heard plenty of criticism along the way.
Remember that you choose what to keep. You can listen fully to feedback and still decide most of it does not fit.
Today, invite feedback on something you are already fairly confident about. It is a good test of how open you can stay.
When you catch yourself sulking after criticism, name it with humour rather than shame. Then take one small step forward.
Ten weeks done. Write down three pieces of feedback you used well over these weeks, and what each one changed.
Start to see yourself as someone who can be corrected without falling apart. That is a strength, not a softness.
Notice how people respond when you take feedback well. Often they become more honest and more generous with you.
Look for one area where feedback has quietly made you better this season. Let yourself enjoy that, rather than rushing to the next fix.
Growth needs outside eyes. You cannot see all of your own blind spots, and that is simply part of being human.
Today, ask for feedback in a way that makes it easy for others: "What's one thing that would make this better?"
Consider writing yourself a short reminder for tough feedback days, something like "This is information, and I can use it."
Notice whether you are kinder to yourself after mistakes now. Self-respect makes it far easier to hear hard things.
When you slip back into defensiveness, and you sometimes will, treat it as a reminder to pause rather than a failure.
Share one thing you have learned about hearing feedback with someone else who struggles with it. Passing it on helps it stick.
Plan a simple routine for future feedback: breathe, listen, ask, thank, reflect, choose one action.
Twelve weeks in. Picture the next piece of difficult feedback you might receive. What do you now trust yourself to do with it?
Expect the sting to return now and then. Feeling it is fine. Being ruled by it is what you have been outgrowing.
Choose one area of your life where you would like to keep inviting honest comments. Decide who you might ask and when.
Look back at the person who began these notes. You can still feel hurt by criticism, but you are steadier in the middle of it.
Remember that the goal was never to stop caring what others think. It was to care in a way that helps you grow.
That brings these ninety days to an end. Keep listening, keep sorting the useful from the rest, and keep growing. You can hear hard things and stay whole.
